promptText: All children should study a foreign language in school, starting in the earliest grades. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement?

phases.correct: The mandating of foreign language acquisition in early childhood education.
distractors: Whether learning a second language is genuinely useful in adult life.
The most effective classroom methods for teaching vocabulary to children.
The dominance of English as the world's principal second language.

phases.correct: The necessity of preserving foundational native language skills.
distractors: Young children should master reading and writing before anything else.
The belief that small children cannot concentrate on two languages.
Ensuring that every pupil achieves a good grade in their own language.

phases.correct: By ensuring young learners establish robust cognitive frameworks in a single language before additional systems are layered upon them.
distractors: By giving children more time to practise their reading and spelling.
By preventing pupils from becoming confused between two grammars.
Through allowing teachers to concentrate on one subject at a time.

phases.correct: Educational models that delay intensive foreign language instruction until native literacy benchmarks are secured.
distractors: Schools teaching a foreign language for only one hour each week.
Parents speaking exclusively their own language at home.
Countries that begin foreign language lessons in secondary school.

phases.correct: Postponing bilingualism actively guarantees missing the period of highest natural phonetic absorption.
distractors: Older pupils often find learning a new language rather boring.
Teenagers already have too many other subjects to study.
Children who start late may never speak with perfect grammar.

phases.correct: The exploitation of the critical window of childhood neuroplasticity.
distractors: Young children are able to learn languages much more easily.
The view that early learners will secure better jobs in future.
Making school more enjoyable by introducing a foreign culture.

phases.correct: By capitalising on the brain's innate capacity for effortless phonological and grammatical acquisition before that faculty diminishes.
distractors: By starting lessons early so that children have more years to practise.
By making children more interested in other countries and cultures.
Through employing native speakers to teach in primary schools.

phases.correct: Highly successful bilingual immersion programmes in which infants acquire a second language through ordinary play and instruction.
distractors: Primary schools introducing weekly French or Mandarin lessons.
Children watching cartoons in a foreign language at home.
Families moving abroad so their children become bilingual.

phases.correct: Poorly designed early language programmes can induce academic anxiety and produce superficial competence in both languages.
distractors: Primary teachers are seldom qualified to teach a foreign language.
Schools may not have enough hours in the timetable.
Some parents object to their children learning another language.

phases.correct: Policymakers must introduce foreign languages in the earliest grades through play-based immersion while simultaneously safeguarding intensive native-language literacy.
distractors: Foreign languages should be taught early, but only for a short period each week.
Children should master their own language first and begin a second at eleven.
Each family should decide when their own child begins a foreign language.

phases.correct: Optimal cognitive development requires the neurological benefits of early bilingualism without sacrificing the structural grounding of a mother tongue.
distractors: Because children who speak two languages will find better employment.
Since the world is now globalised and everyone must communicate.
Because young children learn far more quickly than adults do.

promptText: Children today spend more time watching television than they did in the past. Describe some of the advantages and disadvantages of television for children.

phases.correct: The escalating consumption of broadcast media by adolescents.
distractors: Whether television is more harmful to children than the internet.
The techniques broadcasters use to hold a young viewer's attention.
The declining amount of time children now spend reading books.

phases.correct: The educational potential of high-quality programming.
distractors: Television can teach children a great many interesting facts.
The belief that documentaries are better than cartoons.
Ensuring that children watch only programmes made for their age.

phases.correct: By democratising access to global knowledge and diverse cultural narratives.
distractors: By showing children pictures of places they will never visit.
By keeping young viewers quietly occupied for several hours.
Through helping children improve their listening and vocabulary.

phases.correct: Exposing developing minds to advanced scientific documentaries and historical broadcasts.
distractors: Children watching educational cartoons that teach the alphabet.
Families sitting together to watch the evening news.
Schools showing films to classes on a Friday afternoon.

phases.correct: This passive consumption inherently limits active physical engagement and real-world problem-solving.
distractors: Not every television programme is genuinely educational.
Children may struggle to remember what they have watched.
Some documentaries are far too difficult for young viewers.

phases.correct: The detrimental impact on physical and social development.
distractors: Watching too much television is bad for a child's eyesight.
The idea that children should be playing outdoors instead.
Parents using the television as a convenient babysitter.

phases.correct: By catalysing sedentary behaviours and reducing organic interpersonal communication.
distractors: By keeping children sitting indoors for hours every evening.
By exposing young viewers to violent and unsuitable scenes.
Through preventing families from talking during mealtimes.

phases.correct: Rising rates of childhood obesity and delayed social skills in highly digitised households.

Pupils arriving at school tired after watching late-night programmes.

Obesity is caused mainly by diet rather than by television.
Modern programmes are far better made than those of the past.

phases.correct: While the educational potential of television offers real value, it must be carefully managed with strict parental oversight to mitigate the risks of unregulated, sedentary screen time.
distractors: Children should be permitted to watch only educational programmes.

Parents should remove the television from the home altogether.

phases.correct: Optimal human development requires a balance between rapid digital cognitive stimulation and essential physical and social maturation.
distractors: Because television has both good and bad effects on young children.

Ensuring that universities maintain their international reputation.

Through requiring every candidate to sit an entrance examination.
